chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Global Central Banks India Watches

lessons.title: The US Fed: Why Its Decisions Move Dalal Street

body.text: The US Federal Reserve sets the price of the dollar, the currency the whole world borrows, saves and trades in. When the Fed tightens, global money flows back towards the US; when it eases, money flows out in search of higher returns. India feels every one of those swings through foreign investor flows, the rupee, bond yields and the stock market, often before the RBI has said a word.

children.text: Chapters 1 to 3 kept the focus on the RBI. Chapter 4 looks outward at the central banks that India's markets watch most closely. We start with the most powerful of them all, and explain why a decision taken in Washington at 11:30 pm Indian time can decide how the Nifty opens the next morning.
What the Fed Is and What It Aims For

markDefs.definition: The US Federal Reserve's legal goals of maximum employment and stable prices, set by Congress. The Fed interprets stable prices as 2% inflation over time.

children.text: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank, created in 1913. Unlike the RBI's single inflation target, the Fed works under a
dual mandate
from Congress: maximum employment and stable prices, which it defines as inflation of 2% over time.

federal funds rate
, the overnight rate at which US banks lend to each other. It works much like the RBI's repo rate, but because the dollar is the world's main reserve currency, its effects spread far beyond America.

body.text: The Fed and the RBI are not in lockstep, but they cannot drift too far apart for long. If the Fed hikes while the RBI cuts, the interest rate gap narrows, foreign money leaves Indian bonds and the rupee weakens. That is why Indian bond traders watch US Treasury yields almost as closely as RBI statements.

body.title: What Happens to the Rate Gap?
body.prompt: India's 10-year G-Sec yield is 6.96%. Suppose a hawkish Fed pushes the US 10-year Treasury yield up to 5.00%, while Indian yields stay unchanged. What is the new interest rate differential, in percentage points?
body.explanation: 6.96% minus 5.00% = 1.96 percentage points, down from about 2.23 points when the US yield was 4.73%. A foreign investor now earns less extra yield for taking on rupee risk, so some will sell Indian bonds and move money to the US. That selling pushes Indian yields up and the rupee down, which is how a Fed decision tightens Indian financial conditions without the RBI moving.

children.text: Case 1: A Big Fed Cut Lifts India, September 2024

The Fed announced its 50 basis point cut late on 18 September 2024, Indian time. Indian markets digested it over the next two sessions, and on 20 September, the Sensex surged 1,359.51 points, or 1.63%, to a record close of 84,544.31, while the Nifty 50 rose 375.15 points to a record close of 25,790.95. Cheaper US money and the prospect of more cuts made emerging markets like India more attractive to global investors.

body.title: Size Up the Rally
body.prompt: On 20 September 2024 the Nifty 50 rose 375.15 points to close at 25,790.95. What was the percentage gain for the day? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Previous close = 25,790.95 − 375.15 = 25,415.80. Gain = 375.15 ÷ 25,415.80 × 100 = 1.48%. A strong day for a large, diversified index, driven largely by a decision taken in Washington.

children.text: Case 2: The Hawkish Cut, December 2024

On 18 December 2024, the Fed cut rates by another 25 basis points, to 4.25% to 4.50%. Markets expected the cut. What they did not expect was the dot plot: Fed officials projected only two cuts in all of 2025, fewer than hoped.

On 19 December, the Sensex fell 964 points, or 1.2%, to 79,218, and the Nifty 50 fell 1.02% to 23,951, its fourth straight losing session. As with the RBI's June 2025 decision you studied in Chapter 2, the rate move mattered less than the guidance about what comes next.

body.title: Name the Chart
body.textWithBlank: The Fed's chart showing each official's projection for future interest rates is known as the dot ___.
body.explanation: The dot plot. Published four times a year with the Fed's Summary of Economic Projections, it shows where each FOMC participant expects rates to be. In December 2024, fewer projected cuts turned a rate cut into a market sell-off.

children.text: Case 3: The Warsh Fed and India's 2026 Squeeze

By 2026 the pressure had reversed. Energy prices and sticky inflation kept US CPI around 3.4%, and the new Fed Chair signalled readiness to tighten. At the same time, the West Asia conflict pushed oil higher. For India, the combination was painful.
Record foreign selling:

FPIs pulled out a net ₹2.37 lakh crore from Indian equities in 2026 up to mid-September, already more than the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in all of 2025. They sold ₹13,138 crore in the first two weeks of September alone.
A weaker rupee:
the rupee hit a record low of 96.52 in May and was still past 95 per dollar in September.
Pressure on the RBI:
with the Fed leaning towards hikes, SBI Research expected the RBI to hike too, in October and December, to protect the rupee and fight inflation.

body.title: How Much Bigger Is 2026's Exodus?
body.prompt: FPIs withdrew ₹1.66 lakh crore from Indian equities in all of 2025 and ₹2.37 lakh crore in 2026 up to mid-September. By what percentage does 2026's outflow already exceed 2025's? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (₹2.37 lakh crore − ₹1.66 lakh crore) ÷ ₹1.66 lakh crore × 100 = 42.8%. And the year was not over. Higher US yields, a strong dollar and costly oil made emerging markets less attractive across the board, not just India.

body.title: Why Would the RBI Follow the Fed?
body.question: In September 2026, the Fed looks set to hike while India's own inflation is also rising. Why might the RBI feel pressure to hike as well?
options: The RBI is legally required to match every Fed decision
If the Fed hikes and the RBI does not, the rate gap narrows, capital flows out and the rupee weakens, adding to imported inflation
The Fed sets India's inflation target
Indian banks borrow directly from the Fed
body.explanation: The RBI sets policy for India's own inflation target and is not bound by the Fed. But a narrowing rate gap pushes foreign money out, weakens the rupee and makes imports like oil more expensive, which feeds Indian inflation. When domestic inflation is already rising, a hawkish Fed strengthens the case for the RBI to tighten too.

body.title: Go Deeper: Why the Dollar Gives the Fed Global Reach

children.text: Most global trade, commodity pricing and cross-border borrowing happens in US dollars. Crude oil is priced in dollars. Many emerging market companies borrow in dollars. Central banks, including the RBI, hold large parts of their reserves in US Treasury bonds.

So when the Fed raises rates, the cost of dollar borrowing rises everywhere, the dollar tends to strengthen, and countries that import oil or owe dollar debts come under strain. When the Fed cuts, the pressure eases. This is why economists sometimes call the Fed the world's central bank, even though its mandate is purely American.

body.title: The Morning After a Fed Hike
body.scenario: Suppose the Fed raises rates by 25 basis points to 3.75% to 4.00% on the night of 16 September 2026, and the dot plot shows most officials expecting one more hike this year. You wake up in Mumbai at 7 am with markets opening at 9:15.
body.prompt: What would you expect for the rupee, the Nifty IT index, bank stocks and the 10-year G-Sec yield? What does it mean for the RBI's October meeting?
body.modelAnswer: A hike was widely expected, so the dot plot matters more than the move itself. A signal of another hike is hawkish. The rupee would likely weaken as the dollar strengthens and the rate gap narrows. The 10-year G-Sec yield would likely rise, tracking higher US yields and expectations of RBI tightening. Bank stocks and other rate-sensitives could fall on higher yields and more FPI selling. Nifty IT is mixed: a weaker rupee boosts rupee earnings, but tighter US financial conditions can slow client spending, and TCS earns nearly half its revenue from North America. For the RBI's October meeting, a hawkish Fed strengthens the case for a hike, especially with Indian inflation projected to peak at 5.9% and the rupee near record lows. But if the Fed signals it is done after one move, the reaction could be much milder, and the RBI would have more room to wait.

Check how the rupee and the 10-year G-Sec yield opened the next morning

points: The Fed runs a dual mandate of maximum employment and 2% inflation, and sets the federal funds rate, held at 3.50% to 3.75% since December 2025.
Because the dollar is the world's reserve currency, Fed decisions move global capital flows, the dollar and bond yields everywhere.
Fed moves reach India through FPI flows, the rupee, G-Sec yields, the RBI's room to act and demand for Indian IT services.
The Fed's 50 basis point cut in September 2024 helped push the Nifty to a record; its hawkish cut in December 2024 sent the Nifty down 1.02%.
In 2026, a hawkish Warsh Fed, 3.4% US inflation and high oil prices coincided with record FPI equity outflows of ₹2.37 lakh crore by mid-September.
A hawkish Fed narrows the India-US rate gap and strengthens the case for RBI tightening, even though the RBI sets policy for India's own goals.
